set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Declining referrals from Google search account for most of the recent fall in human traffic to Wikipedia.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Wikipedia's search referral traffic would have declined even if generative AI had not emerged.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Machine traffic to Wikimedia projects will eventually exceed human traffic.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: AI systems that summarise Wikipedia content without linking to it reduce the number of readers who go on to become editors.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: The most serious risk to Wikimedia from AI is the cost of serving machine traffic, rather than the loss of influence over how knowledge is produced.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Wikimedia is on the same trajectory that Stack Overflow followed after 2022.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Stack Overflow declined for reasons specific to programming questions that do not apply to an encyclopedia.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Wikipedia's decision to remain a text-based medium has cost it readers who prefer video.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Readers who prefer quick, low-effort answers have a legitimate need that Wikipedia has not met.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Large AI models trained mainly on English Wikipedia present its coverage as global default knowledge.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Open licensing has allowed AI developers to take value from Wikimedia while returning little in exchange.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Large-scale AI training on Wikipedia content is exactly the kind of reuse that Wikimedia's open licences were written to permit.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Most people who now rely on Wikipedia-derived content do not know that they are doing so.

set_name: Diagnosis: the state of the knowledge loop
statement: Paywalls, bot-blocking, and AI-generated web content are making it harder for editors to find citable sources.
Wikimedia's current approach to AI companies is closer to passive acceptance than to active negotiation.
Rate-limiting AI crawlers protects Wikimedia infrastructure at an acceptable cost to openness.
Restricting access to Wikimedia content in response to AI scraping would do more damage to the mission than the scraping does.
Wikimedia should offer some AI companies exclusive access to its content in exchange for higher payment.
Keeping access open without conditions remains the right approach, since reuse eventually returns value to the commons.
Wikimedia should set conditions on how AI systems use its content, rather than granting permission in advance through open licences.
Wikimedia has enough influence over AI companies to negotiate terms those companies would otherwise refuse.
The volume of openly shared content is no longer an adequate measure of the health of the knowledge commons.
When openness and the financial sustainability of Wikimedia conflict, sustainability should take precedence.
Wikimedia Enterprise shows that large-scale commercial use of the commons can be structured through negotiated agreements.
Wikimedia Enterprise revenue, at 4% of Foundation income, is too small to change how AI companies behave.
Taking an active political stance toward AI companies would damage Wikimedia's reputation for neutrality.
Wikimedia should treat its relationship with AI companies as a negotiation between parties whose interests conflict.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: AI systems that draw on Wikimedia content should display visible attribution to Wikipedia in their answers.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Attribution requirements cannot be enforced against large AI companies, so Wikimedia should direct its effort elsewhere.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: AI developers should be required to disclose which Wikimedia content they used to train their models.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: The Share Alike condition should be redesigned to cover AI models trained on Wikimedia content.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Applying Share Alike to the outputs of AI models would prove unworkable in practice.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: AI companies that use Wikimedia content at scale should pay for that use.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Requirements to attribute and link matter more to Wikimedia's future than payments from AI companies.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: AI platforms should share data with Wikimedia communities about what readers ask them.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Accepting usage data from AI platforms would make Wikimedia's editorial priorities dependent on commercial partners.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Access to Wikimedia content at scale should be conditional on meeting reciprocity requirements.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Wikimedia should apply the same reuse conditions to every AI developer, rather than negotiating agreements one at a time.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Reciprocity agreements negotiated company by company will not shift the norms of the wider ecosystem.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Wikimedia should seek a seat in the bodies that set AI ecosystem protocols such as MCP.

set_name: Reciprocity and the terms of reuse
statement: Wikimedia should publish rules covering how it collects, documents, and licenses the datasets it creates.
Wikimedia should build interfaces through which readers reach the commons directly, rather than relying on search engines and AI assistants.
Building reader-facing AI interfaces falls outside the mission of an encyclopedia project.
Delegating the reader-facing interface to search engines was a reasonable choice during the search era.
Wikimedia will lose its direct relationship with readers unless it operates an interface of its own.
Any AI interface Wikimedia builds should send readers to Wikipedia articles rather than answering in place of them.
An AI interface that answers readers' questions directly would reduce the number of people who go on to edit.
Wikimedia should support several competing AI interfaces rather than building one official product.
Wikimedia should build its own conversational AI assistant.
Building AI interfaces would divert resources from maintaining the encyclopedia itself.
Wikimedia's credibility with readers depends on it not being seen as a company that builds AI products.
Readers who receive accurate Wikipedia-derived answers from an AI assistant are being served well, even when they never visit Wikipedia.
Wikimedia should aim to be one of the main interfaces through which people reach knowledge by 2030.
Wikimedia should build AI interfaces jointly with public AI developers rather than on its own.
Wikimedia should publish machine-readable signals about the editorial quality and review state of its content.
Wikimedia should develop Wikidata as the primary structured knowledge layer that AI systems draw on.
Wikimedia should fund a technical environment for AI experimentation that is separate from production infrastructure.
Wikimedia's production infrastructure is poorly suited to rapid experimentation with AI tools.
A state-of-the-art open AI model is a prerequisite for the rest of Wikimedia's AI strategy.
Wikimedia should contribute training data and reciprocity standards to public AI models built by partners, rather than training a model itself.
Wikimedia should withhold its name from AI models whose behaviour it cannot control.
Wikimedia should develop Wikimedia Enterprise into the main channel through which AI systems reach its content.
Wikimedia should recruit content partners specifically to supply data that AI systems currently lack.
Wikimedia should fund crowdsourced collection of scarce data types, such as recordings of spoken language.
Wikimedia should prioritise AI tools that support existing editors over tools that serve readers.
Building AI tools for editors will accelerate the decline in the number of active editors.
Wikimedia should adopt machine learning models built by others rather than developing that capacity in-house.
Wikimedia's AI technology roadmap should follow the Global Majority Technology Priorities set in 2024.
Wikimedia's distinctive value lies in the human process that produces its content, rather than in the content itself.
AI tools should help editors reach judgments rather than make editorial judgments in their place.
Editors should be permitted to use AI tools to draft article text.
AI-generated content submitted without disclosure damages the reliability of Wikipedia.
Wikipedia should require editors to disclose when they have used AI tools to produce content.
The decline in new editors is driven mainly by falling reader traffic rather than by conditions inside the editing community.
Recruiting new editors should take priority over developing AI technology.
Volunteer editors should hold a formal role in deciding Wikimedia's AI strategy.
Wikimedia's AI response should be led by institutional staff rather than by volunteers.
Wikimedia communities respond to sudden influxes of readers by protecting articles rather than by recruiting contributors.
Wikimedia should design AI-related volunteer tasks that people find worth doing, rather than tasks that mainly involve repetitive review.
Automating editorial work with AI will narrow the range of viewpoints represented on Wikipedia.
Wikipedia's model of negotiated consensus among editors cannot be reproduced by an AI system.
Wikimedia should accept a smaller editing community if AI tools let it maintain the same quality of content.
Machine traffic makes up a larger share of total traffic on small-language Wikipedias than on the largest ones.
Small-language Wikipedias matter to AI developers because they are often the only structured source in those languages.
The communities maintaining small-language Wikipedias have the least capacity to respond to pressure from AI systems.
Uncorrected machine translation has become a serious problem for several African-language Wikipedias.
Wikimedia should be willing to close a language project when AI-generated content threatens the integrity of that language.
AI systems trained on Wikimedia freeze the movement's existing gaps in coverage into global default knowledge.
Wikimedia should commit a fixed share of its AI investment to Global Majority communities.
Technical solutions designed for well-resourced communities will widen inequality within the movement by default.
Solutions built for Global Majority communities will also serve Global North communities, while the reverse does not hold.
Global Majority partners should hold decision-making authority over the AI mission, not only a role in delivering it.
Directing AI investment by geography would slow the movement's technical progress overall.
Removing legal barriers to reuse has not produced equity in access to knowledge.
Wikimedia's citation and verifiability policies exclude forms of knowledge that are not published in writing.
Wikipedia should accept oral sources as citations on topics where written sources do not exist.
No single Wikimedia organisation can carry out an AI strategy for the movement on its own.
The Wikimedia Foundation should lead the movement's response to AI.
A coordinating body spanning movement entities, volunteers, and outside partners should be established for AI work.
Creating another movement-wide coordinating body will produce meetings rather than results.
The Wikimedia Endowment should provide seed funding for the movement's AI work.
AI work should be funded jointly by several organisations, so that no single funder sets its direction.
Movement organisations should fund AI work from core budgets rather than through grants.
Smaller Wikimedia affiliates can move faster on AI experimentation than the largest organisations.
Wikimedia should partner with public AI developers such as Apertus, OLMo, and Pleias.
Partnering with named AI developers would compromise Wikimedia's standing as a neutral source.
Movement leaders should take public positions in external debates about AI governance.
Wikimedia should present a position on AI governance at the 2027 Geneva AI Summit.
Wikimedia CH should open space for the movement to act in Switzerland rather than lead the work itself.
Wikimedia should spend the next two years building agreement across the movement before committing to a technical direction.
